summary: This document extends the ForCES protocol with a table range operation and an extension for error handling, to ease programmability and improve wire efficiency. It updates the semantics in RFCs 5810 and 7121.

eli5.summary: Routers have a thinking part and a doing part, and ForCES lets them talk. This RFC adds a way to ask about many table rows at once and report mistakes more clearly.

questions: what is the forces extendedresult tlv
how does forces dump a large table
subtitle: Two small ForCES additions: ask for a range of table rows in one request, and get far more precise error codes back.

tldr.problem: In ForCES, fetching or deleting many table rows meant dumping the whole table or sending thousands of requests, and the generic error codes made debugging slow.
tldr.mechanism: A new TABLERANGE-TLV selects a start and end row index in one GET or DEL, and a new EXTENDEDRESULT-TLV carries a 32-bit result code with an optional cause string. The RFC also describes how a large table dump is split over several response messages.
tldr.outcome: The extensions are backward compatible and make controllers simpler and the wire traffic smaller. The RFC updates RFC 5810 and RFC 7121.

today: RFC 7391 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5810 and RFC 7121. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why ForCES Needed Extensions
sections.content:
In the ForCES architecture a Control Element (CE) tells a Forwarding Element (FE) what to do. Implementation and deployment experience showed the need for a few small extensions, to ease programmability and to improve wire efficiency of some transactions. This RFC extends the semantics of the ForCES protocol in RFC 5810.

It makes three changes: a table range operation, additional error codes with a new TLV to carry details, and a clarification of how an FE answers a GET of a large table that does not fit in a single Protocol Layer (PL) message. The first two are described as small and backward compatible.
sections.eli5: People who built ForCES found some jobs were slow and some error messages were vague. This RFC adds a few small tools to fix that without breaking anything that already worked.

sections.title: The Problems Being Solved
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example of a table with 1 million sparsely populated rows, of which 2000 sit between row indices 23 and 10023. To get those rows, a control application could dump the whole table and filter, send up to 10000 requests while incrementing the index by one, or use ForCES batching if it knows which rows exist. The RFC calls all of these tedious and wasteful of compute and wire resources.

For errors, RFC 5810 defines only a generic set of codes. A single code such as E_NOT_SUPPORTED can stand for many different causes in the FE, so the caller has to guess from the request, which makes debugging more time consuming.
sections.eli5: Imagine you want 2000 cards out of a giant box. You could carry the whole box, or fetch one card at a time. Both are silly. And if someone just says 'no' without saying why, you cannot fix the problem.

sections.title: The Table Range TLV
sections.content:
The new TABLERANGE-TLV has type ID 0x0117 and is associated with the PATH-DATA-TLV in the same way the KEYINFO-TLV is. It holds a 32-bit start index and a 32-bit end index. A start index of 0 means the beginning of the table, and an end index of 0xFFFFFFFF means the last entry.

A request sets the new path flag F_SELTABRANGE (0x2, bit 1) to say the TLV is present. The flag can only be used in a GET or DEL and is mutually exclusive with F_SELKEY. The FE MUST check that the path points to a defined, indexed table component, and MUST reject violations with E_INVALID_TFLAGS. Combining a TABLERANGE-TLV with a KEYINFO-TLV, or nesting several TABLERANGE-TLVs, is discouraged for simplicity.

If at least one row exists, the response carries the rows inside a SPARSEDATA-TLV, with an index for each row. A range delete succeeds if any requested row is deleted, and returns an error only if none can be deleted. An empty range gives E_EMPTY.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking for rows one by one, you say 'give me rows 11 to 23'. The answer comes back as the rows that really exist, each labelled with its row number.

sections.title: Extended Error Codes
sections.content:
The new EXTENDEDRESULT-TLV (type ID 0x0118) carries a 32-bit Result Value followed by an optional cause content. This is a superset of the 8-bit RESULT-TLV value in RFC 5810; the first 256 codes are common to both. The cause is expected to be a UTF-8 string meant for a human operator, and it is recommended that it not exceed 32 bytes. The TLV is 32-bit aligned.

Nine new codes are defined, 0x18 to 0x20, such as E_TIMED_OUT, E_INVALID_TFLAGS, E_BUSY, E_EMPTY and the catch-all E_UNKNOWN. Codes 0x100 to 0x200 are reserved for private vendor use; the FE and CE sides must both understand them and avoid conflicts.
sections.eli5: Before, an error was like a short note saying 'problem'. Now it can be a longer label plus a few words of explanation, so a person can see what actually went wrong.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and the FEPO
sections.content:
To stay compatible, the FE Protocol Object (FEPO) LFB is updated to version 1.2, with a new component ID 16 (EResultAdmin) and a capability component ID 32 (EResultCapab). An FE advertises what it supports in the capability table. An FE that handles both modes starts with the lowest common denominator and answers with plain RESULT-TLVs.

A master CE can write 2 to EResultAdmin to make the FE send only EXTENDEDRESULT-TLVs, or write 1 to switch back. An FE that does not support the requested mode MUST refuse with E_NOT_SUPPORTED. An FE advertising FEPO version 1.2 MUST support EXTENDEDRESULT-TLVs at minimum. How CEs in a high availability setup agree on strict mode is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The new, chattier error style is off by default. A boss controller can switch it on once it knows the helper understands it, so old and new equipment can still work together.

sections.title: Dumping Large Tables
sections.content:
A GET on a table with millions of rows cannot fit in one message, and RFC 5810 does not describe this well. The FE answers with several GET-RESPONSE messages that all reuse the request's correlator. Transaction flags mark the position: the first has Start of Transaction (SOT), the middle ones Middle of Transaction (MOT), and the last End of Transaction (EOT).

The final EOT message MUST NOT carry data. It carries a RESULT-TLV, mirroring the empty commit message of ForCES two-phase commit.
sections.eli5: A huge table is sent like a long letter in many envelopes, all with the same reference number. The last envelope is empty and just says 'that was everything'.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA registered the two new TLVs and two new path flags, and added FEPO LFB version 1.2. A new 'EXTENDEDRESULT-TLV Result Values' sub-registry mirrors codes 0x00 to 0xFF. Future allocations in the range 0x21 to 0xFE must be made there. Ranges 0x21 to 0xFE and 0x201 to 0xFFFFFFFF are Unassigned under Specification Required, with a Designated Expert who must ensure existing deployments are not broken.

The security section is a single sentence: the considerations of RFC 5810 apply here as well.
sections.eli5: The official list of codes was updated so nobody reuses the same number for different things. For safety, the old ForCES rules still apply.

fields.name: Start Index
fields.desc: First row; 0 means the beginning of the table.

fields.name: End Index
fields.desc: Last row; 0xFFFFFFFF means the last entry.

items.label: E_TIMED_OUT
items.desc: A timeout occurred while processing the message.

items.label: E_UNKNOWN
items.desc: Generic catch-all; carries a string explaining the error.
